edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous. Contains orellanine, a nephrotoxin that causes delayed kidney failure. Onset is dangerously deceptive: there are typically no or only minor early symptoms, with renal failure developing days to weeks (commonly 2-3 weeks, with a reported range of about 2 days to 3 weeks) after ingestion, by which time damage is often irreversible and may require dialysis or kidney transplant. Cooking, drying, and freezing do NOT destroy the toxin. Never eat any Cortinarius (webcap).
description: Cortinarius orellanus, the Fool's Webcap, is a deadly orange-brown webcap whose toxin orellanine causes severe, delayed kidney failure days to weeks after ingestion. The mushroom has a tawny to rusty orange-brown cap, widely spaced rusty-coloured gills, and a cortina (cobweb-like partial veil) typical of the genus. Because early symptoms are absent or mild, poisoning is frequently recognised only after irreversible renal damage has occurred.
distribution: Found in Europe, growing in deciduous woodland associated with broadleaf trees such as oak, beech, and birch.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible chanterelles are sometimes confused with the orange-brown cap; chanterelles have blunt false gills (forking ridges) running down the stem, no cortina, a pale to yellowish spore print, and a fruity apricot smell, whereas C. orellanus has true gills, a cobweb cortina, and a rusty-brown spore print.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius rubellus (deadly webcap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly orellanine-containing webcap, similarly toxic; differs by its more conical/umbonate cap and association with conifers, but both are deadly and should be avoided.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Cortinarius (webcap) species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Many webcaps look broadly similar with rusty-brown spores and a cortina; because deadly orellanine-containers are nearly impossible to separate reliably in the field, no Cortinarius should be eaten.
